newsitem.title: USA: Major drugs search at Ohio prison.
newsitem.headline: Major drugs search at Ohio prison.

text.p: One in five inmates at an Ohio prison tested positive for drugs on Tuesday during a major search of the facility aimed at sending a warning to inmates and staff, officials said.

A special team of 200 prison officials and state police with 10 drug-sniffing dogs searched the Mansfield Correctional Institution, 60 miles (95 km) southwest of Cleveland, after random tests showed an abnormally high rate of positive tests.
Prison employees' cars were also searched as officials sought to pinpoint how drugs were being brought in.

Officials at Ohio's Department of Rehabilitation and Correction said they believed most were brought in by visitors or sent in packages. Last year, 54 prison visitors and six employees were arrested in connection with drug smuggling.
"We wanted to send a message to the inmates and staff that we are not going to put up with this kind of thing," he said.
"They do some ingenious things, like taking the bottoms out of tennis shoes, putting drugs in and mailing them in for Christmas," said department official Joe Andrews.
Monthly random tests showed percentages of positive results were significantly higher than at Ohio's other 28 prisons, said Andrews.
Similar routine tests at other Ohio facilities produced an average of three to five percent, but at Mansfield the rates were as high as 19 percent, he said in a telephone interview.
All 2,059 inmates were due to be tested, Andrews said. By late afternoon, 275 of 1,393 tested -- one in nearly five -- had tested positive, mainly for marijuana.
Offenders would be restricted to their cells or sent to a maximum-security facility. Mansfield is a close-security prison, between maximum and medium security.
Andrews said the state was baffled as to why drug use was higher at Mansfield. "We hope to get some idea from this massive search," he said.
"This is a rather rural prison. We have found folks throwing tennis balls (containing drugs) over the prison fence. We want people to know we're onto them."
